bodies.intuition: Writing evaluations by hand is slow, and the behaviours worth measuring keep multiplying. So use a model to generate the test items, and a model to filter them, and check a sample by hand. It scales the one thing that had been the bottleneck, and it introduces a dependency worth naming: the tests now share a source with the thing being tested.
bodies.engineer: It works well enough to have found real behaviours — that larger and more RLHF-trained models express stronger stated preferences about their own continuation, for instance — which is the kind of finding that would not have been looked for by hand. The quality control that makes it usable is a human-labelled sample of the generated items, reported as an agreement rate. Without that number the evaluation is unfalsifiable, because nobody knows what fraction of it measures what it claims.
bodies.math: Shared provenance is a correlated-error problem. If the generator and the subject fail in the same way — the same blind spot, the same misreading of an ambiguous term — the evaluation will not detect it, and the size of that shared region is unknown and unbounded from inside the pipeline. So a high score carries less information than the same score from an independently written test, by an amount nobody can compute, which is a reason to use both rather than to abandon either.
